title: No greater love
hook: greater love hath no man than this, that he lay down his life for his friends

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was washing feet, love that kneels down. Your line was wash feet. Today, the same night, a little later, and the week's last day.

The feet are washed. The basin is put away. In John's Gospel, Jesus keeps talking to his friends late into that last evening, and it reads like someone saying everything that matters before a door closes. Somewhere in that long talk comes one sentence about love. It sets a bar, and it's high. And in the next breath, it changes what the friends are called.
screen: `THE BASIN IS PUT AWAY.` → `A LONG TALK BEFORE A DOOR CLOSES.` → `ONE SENTENCE SETS THE BAR.`

segments.voice: First, the command it explains: "This is my commandment, That ye love one another, as I have loved you." Not as much as you can manage. As I have loved you. Second, the sentence itself: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." In John's story it's said the night before the crucifixion, and Christian tradition hears it pointing straight at the next day: he is describing what he's about to do. Third, the word friends. A moment later: "Henceforth I call you not servants," but "I have called you friends." The Greek is a form of philos, the friend-love from earlier this block. The men whose feet he washed like a servant, he now calls friends; the rank goes the other way from what the room expected. Fourth, the small version. Dying for a friend is not a request that comes to everyone, and some readers hear a quieter meaning: a life can be laid down an hour at a time. A night shift at a sickbed. A weekend given up. A plan let go so a friend can have theirs. And the week of love's voices: clinging, holding on, the friend, seal, First John, even them, wash feet, and now lay it down. Ruth stayed, Jonathan stepped aside, the Song set love against death, John made it the test, and Jesus took the towel and named the bar.
screen: `AS I HAVE LOVED YOU.` · `LAY DOWN HIS LIFE FOR HIS FRIENDS.` · `NOT SERVANTS: FRIENDS.` · `AN HOUR AT A TIME.` · then, large: `NO GREATER LOVE.`

segments.voice: Choose one friend who could use something from you this week, and look at what you were planning to keep for yourself: an evening, a little money, the last word in an argument, the favor you've been saving. Pick one small thing you could set down for them, hold the picture of handing it over, and notice the little cost; that cost is the point. If you pray, you can offer it with their name.
Philos. The friend-love Jesus uses when he calls his followers friends instead of servants, the night he spoke of laying down a life for them. Today's word.
Your line: lay it down. An hour at a time counts too. A week of love's voices, done.

howItsDone: Christian tradition reads John 15:13 as Jesus describing his own death, and the verse is read at some funerals and carved on some memorials to people who died for others.
